summary: Cool Runnings saw a 30% increase in qualified bookings following website, local SEO and conversion work. The project connected useful service and location information with practical tools and a direct enquiry route, helping customers move from finding the business to arranging work.
takeaways: Build around the services and places the business actually covers.
Use local information to answer practical customer questions.
Connect discovery to an enquiry that the business can act on.

sections.body:
Cool Runnings needed to turn local interest into useful enquiries, which meant explaining its landscaping services clearly and helping customers get in touch. The work went beyond making a homepage look finished, because service information, local search and the request process had to work together.

For a landscaping business, a useful enquiry includes the kind of work, the property location and enough context to arrange the next conversation. A visitor comparing companies needs to understand whether the business covers the work before asking for an estimate. Those decisions shaped the site and the content.

The original Cool Runnings case study shows the website and local-search system behind the project.

Cool Runnings’ website gives the services enough detail by presenting them as concrete kinds of work customers can recognise. Service content gives local searches somewhere useful to land and helps the visitor understand what the business can do.

That structure also makes the enquiry more specific. A customer reading about yard maintenance arrives with a different need from someone considering sod installation or rock work. The page should support that distinction instead of sending every visitor through a generic introduction.

The practical lesson for another trade is to start with its actual service list. Find the questions that affect the first conversation and put those answers on the relevant page.

The Cool Runnings content system adds local information with a purpose by bringing together city, service, neighbourhood, weather, frost and growing-season information. The point is to make local pages useful for the work, rather than adding town names to identical copy.

For a landscaping customer, timing and property conditions can affect planning. Local context belongs on a page when it helps explain the service, prepare for a conversation or understand the next step. The page structure, internal links, canonical URLs and sitemap organise that information into a coherent website.

Another industry needs different local detail. An accommodation page needs location and arrival information; a professional practice needs its actual office and appointment process. The content model should follow the business.

Cool Runnings’ website gives visitors something useful before they enquire by including practical guides and calculators alongside the service content. These resources help visitors work through questions rather than leaving them with a service name and a contact button.

A useful tool belongs close to the service it supports. Explain what the output means and which details still need a conversation or site assessment. The website can help a visitor prepare without pretending that a simple calculation is a final professional quote.

For another business, the right resource may be a preparation checklist, a clear scope comparison or an explanation of the booking process. Choose the resource from customer questions, not from a requirement to add something interactive.

Cool Runnings’ conversion work makes the next step direct by connecting the service information to calls and estimate enquiries. A clear next step gives someone who has understood the offer a way to move forward.

For an Okanagan service business, the handoff matters as much as the button. The request needs to reach the right person with the location and work described clearly enough to respond. Website copy, form design and the response process should agree about what happens next.

The same review can expose friction elsewhere: a contact link that is difficult to find on a phone, a form that asks too much or a confirmation that implies a booking before one is agreed.

Cool Runnings saw a 30% increase in qualified bookings following the website, local SEO and conversion work. The work brought service content, local visibility and the enquiry process together around that business goal.

Search visibility and website actions help explain how a site is being used, but they are different measurements. A click can lead to a conversation; it does not establish that a job was booked. Keeping those stages separate makes the reporting useful for business decisions.

The project shows the value of connecting discovery, useful content and a practical enquiry path. It also provides a stronger basis for a consultation than a promise that a new design alone will create more work.

An Okanagan business can apply the Cool Runnings approach by starting with the work it wants to win and building the website around that customer’s questions.

  • Choose the priority services and the area you actually cover.
  • Write useful answers for each service and meaningful local differences.
  • Show relevant work and make the request route easy to complete.
  • Check who receives the enquiry and how the next conversation happens.
  • Track qualified bookings separately from traffic and button taps.

Michael McKerracher’s website design service brings that content, design and search planning together. Additional marketing and branding or workflow implementation can support the business where the next bottleneck sits.

faqs: What was the result of the Cool Runnings website work?

Cool Runnings saw a 30% increase in qualified bookings following the website, local SEO and conversion work. The result refers to jobs and qualified bookings. The work joined service information, location content and an easier enquiry route. Use the case study to understand those decisions, and keep the qualified-booking result distinct from the separate search and traffic measurements. The useful question for another business is which part of its own customer journey needs improvement.
Do I need calculators and a large website to use this approach?

No. Start with useful service information, relevant evidence and a working enquiry route. Add tools or more content when they solve a real customer question and the business can maintain them. Add a tool only when it helps customers assess a real job or prepare a useful request. A small site can start with clear service scope, coverage, relevant work and working contact options. Expand after actual enquiries show where more information would help.
Can the same approach work outside landscaping?

The principles can apply to other service businesses, but the content should change. A clinic needs appointment and practitioner information; an accountant needs scope and preparation details; a trade needs service coverage and a practical estimate request. Adapt the content and enquiry route to the buying decision. A plumber needs urgent and planned-work paths; a professional practice needs service fit and an appropriate first conversation. Carry over the method of connecting discovery, proof and action rather than copying landscaping pages word for word.
How would you apply this approach to my business?

Start by examining the services you want to sell, how suitable customers search and what staff need to turn an enquiry into work. Review the current website and real project evidence, then design the pages and contact journey around those needs. The scope follows the business rather than a fixed set of copied pages.
What should I measure after the new website launches?

Record qualified enquiries and accepted jobs, alongside traffic sources and the pages that produced them when known. Keep the definition of a qualified booking consistent. Review unsuitable requests and missed follow-up as well, since additional traffic has limited value if the team cannot turn appropriate enquiries into work.
